key_facts: **Congenital melanocytic naevi (CMN)** are present at birth or appear in the first months; about 1% of newborns.
Classified by projected adult size: small (<1.5 cm), medium, large (20–40 cm), giant (>40 cm).
Melanoma risk is low for small and medium CMN, higher for **large/giant** (a few per cent, often in childhood).
Multiple CMN or large CMN: MRI for **neurocutaneous melanosis** (NRAS mutations).
Monitor with photographs; refer new nodules, ulceration or rapid change; support families (Caring Matters Now).

sections.title: Overview
blocks: A melanocytic naevus present at birth (or appearing in the first year, "tardive"). About 1% of newborns have one; large/giant ones occur in about 1 in 20,000.

sub: About 1% have a small CMN; large or giant CMN about 1 in 20,000 births.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: **Post-zygotic NRAS mutation** in neural-crest melanoblasts (BRAF in some small CMN). The earlier the mutation, the larger the naevus and the more likely satellites and neurocutaneous melanosis (CNS melanocytes).

ul: **"All congenital moles should be removed"**: most small CMN never cause problems; surgery has its own risks.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: CMN arise from a **mutation in an embryonic melanocyte precursor**, mostly NRAS.

mech.t: A post-zygotic NRAS (or BRAF) mutation in a migrating melanocyte precursor.
Descendant melanocytes populate a patch of skin, sometimes deep into fat and fascia.
mech.caption: Congenital naevus cells extend deep into the dermis and fat, wrapping around follicles, glands, vessels and nerves.

mech.t: Earlier mutation gives larger, deeper naevi and sometimes CNS involvement.
CMN become more raised, hairy and textured with age; some lighten.

histo: Naevus cells extending deep into dermis and around adnexa, vessels and nerves.

ul: **Size by projected adult size (PAS)**: small <1.5 cm; medium 1.5–20 cm (M1 1.5–10 cm, M2 10–20 cm); **large 20–40 cm**; **giant >40 cm**

Head lesions roughly double, and trunk and limb lesions roughly triple, from infancy to adulthood. **A 30 cm trunk CMN at age 5 projects to >40 cm, so it is a giant CMN** ([Case 2](condition:melanocytic-naevi).

Features: brown to black, often hairy, with varied texture. **They become rougher, lumpy, hairier or lighter with time**. These are benign maturation changes (the course point), but a new **firm nodule, ulceration, rapid growth or pain** needs urgent assessment. Also proliferative nodules (benign) occur in infancy.
**Satellite naevi** and **multiple CMN** (≥2 at birth) are markers for **neurocutaneous melanosis/CNS involvement** (seizures, developmental delay, hydrocephalus).

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical, with serial photographs. Biopsy of new nodules. **MRI of brain and spine** (ideally in the first 6 months of life, before myelination, under natural sleep) in children with **≥2 CMN at birth, of any size** (the current UK expert approach; Kinsler). It is not routine for a single CMN without neurological signs.

ul: Brain + spine, ideally < 6 months (natural sleep), if **≥ 2 CMN at birth, any size**; not routine for a single CMN without neurology.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: Café-au-lait macule (flat, no hair, uniform), Becker naevus (acquired, adolescent shoulder, hairy), dermal melanocytosis ("Mongolian spot", blue-grey, sacral), speckled lentiginous naevus (naevus spilus), smooth muscle hamartoma, and plexiform neurofibroma with overlying pigment.

ul: **Melanoma risk by size (corrected; related question):** **Small and medium CMN: lifetime melanoma risk is low (<1%)**, similar to or slightly above the general population, and melanoma usually arises after puberty at the junctional edge; **Large/giant CMN: around 2–5% overall (up to 10–15% in the highest-risk group: >40 cm PAS with many satellites/multiple CMN)**. Melanoma often arises in childhood and **deep** in the naevus or in the CNS, which is why surface excision does not remove the risk; The course "5–10%" belongs to the large/giant group, **not** to small/medium CMN
**Refer** (routine to paediatric dermatology; urgent for any new nodule, ulcer or rapid change) for **lifelong surveillance** and MDT input (dermatology, plastics, neurology, psychology).

**Prophylactic excision:** no evidence that it reduces melanoma risk in large/giant CMN (the course point). Surgery is for function, cosmesis or symptoms, as an MDT decision. **Laser** lightens the surface but leaves deep naevus cells and can make surveillance harder. It is not recommended routinely (specialist only).
**Support:** itch (emollients; antihistamines at night if needed); dry, fragile skin; psychological impact and bullying. Point families to *Caring Matters Now* (UK charity for CMN).
Sun protection, and **teach parents what change to report**.

ladder.t: **Small / medium: lifetime melanoma risk < 1%** (usually after puberty, at the edge). **Large / giant: ~2–5%** (up to 10–15% if > 40 cm with many satellites); often **childhood and deep / CNS**.
Paediatric dermatology (routine; **urgent** for nodule, ulcer, rapid change) for lifelong MDT surveillance (dermatology, plastics, neurology, psychology).
Teach families what change to report; photograph regularly; sun protection; psychological support.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Prophylactic excision**: No evidence it reduces melanoma risk in large / giant CMN.

refer.t: New firm nodule, ulceration, rapid growth or pain within a CMN.
Scalp or multiple CMN with headaches, vomiting or seizures: same-day paediatrics.
≥ 2 CMN at birth or large / giant with satellites: MRI and specialist surveillance.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: A new firm nodule, ulceration, rapid growth or pain within a CMN: **urgent** referral.
Two or more CMN at birth, or a large/giant CMN with satellites: refer for MRI and specialist surveillance.
Melanoma (large/giant), neurocutaneous melanosis, psychosocial impact; proliferative nodules in infancy (usually benign).

pearls: The rough, hairy, raised changes the parent describes are expected. A **hard lump** is not.
If scalp CMN or multiple CMN plus headaches, vomiting or seizures, arrange **same-day** paediatric review.

quiz.q: A 30 cm trunk CMN at age 5: category?

quiz.a: Infants with ≥ 2 CMN at birth (any size).

quiz.q: Does prophylactic excision remove the risk?
